headline: The feared 'Black Monday' isn't showing up: Brent is off ≈1.7% to ≈$108 on Trump's Russia-sanctions waiver while the IRGC's tanker-mine claim stays unconfirmed, China's 4.5% GDP beat has Nasdaq futures up ≈1% and the 10Y has slipped to ≈5.07%, and a heavy regional-bank week opens with Fifth Third's beat and Wintrust tonight.
summary: Oil gap risk fizzled. Late Sunday Dec Brent printed $108.52, then traded $107.60–108.06 in Asia, against Friday's $109.86 settle. WTI briefly dipped under $99. The driver is Friday's waiver of new Russia sanctions, not Hormuz: the IRGC still claims two ≈2M-bbl tankers hit mines, but no major wire has confirmed it and CENTCOM says escorted transits continue. A confirmation is the main upside risk to crude and breakevens today.

Rates: 10Y ≈5.07% (−2 bp), 2Y ≈4.73% (≈flat), 30Y ≈5.41% (CNBC/Trading Economics), so 2s10s ≈34 bp. Term premium is 1.33 pp on the SF Fed model, up from 1.07 a year ago. With the Fed in blackout, FedWatch has an Oct 28 hold at ≈84% and a hike at ≈16%. Supply starts today with $95B 13-week and $82B 26-week bills, then the $13B 20Y reopening Wednesday and the 5Y TIPS Thursday.

China beat: Q3 GDP grew 4.5% y/y (poll 4.4%, Q2 4.3%) and 1.2% q/q. September retail sales rose 1.1% (poll ≈0.6%) and industrial output 5.5% (in line). Fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% YTD, with property investment down 20.6%. Exports, not consumers, did the work. That supports copper (≈$14,480/t LME into LME Week) and risk sentiment, but it lowers the odds of a big stimulus package.

Equities: S&P futures are ≈+0.5% at ≈7,740 and Nasdaq-100 futures ≈+1.0% at ≈29,687 after the Nasdaq's −4.5% week. Europe is the soft spot: the Stoxx 600 is ≈−0.3 to −0.7% and the CAC is down ≈1% after the weekend's French riots (more than 2,000 arrests). The French 10Y is up ≈7 bp, with the OAT–Bund spread ≈137 bp.

Banks: Fifth Third posted adjusted Q3 EPS of $1.13 vs ≈$1.08–1.09 consensus, with NII of $2.28B (+3% q/q) and CET1 at 10.02%. That is its first quarter with Comerica fully integrated, per its 8-K. Wintrust (Chicago) reports after the close ($3.31 / $754.7M est.), then KeyCorp ($0.46) and Capital One on Tuesday, and CME ($2.98 / $1.71B) and Northern Trust Wednesday. The KBW Bank Index needs to break a six-week losing streak, its longest since 2008, and it sits ≈13% below August's record.

Metals: gold is +0.3% at $4,175.60 spot, and Dec futures briefly went above $4,200 as real yields eased. Silver is up ≈1% to ≈$57.5, platinum ≈+1.3% (≈$1,655) and palladium ≈+1.5% (≈$1,133). The structural bid is intact: WGC data show a record $31B of Q3 ETF inflows, and the PBoC bought 23t in September, its biggest month since Oct 2023.
markets_asof: Close ≈3:15 PM CT (indices final; yields, oil and metals are late-session reads, not settles)

calendar.why: It's the first clean quarter with Comerica fully in. The adjusted $1.13 beat and NII +3% q/q set the bar for regional NII stories all week.
The cleanest read of the energy shock on a G10 peer, and it moves the CAD and front-end correlation with US rates.
September was the lowest since Sep 2025. With the 10Y above 5%, mortgage rates are squeezing builders, and a further drop feeds the growth-scare side of the Fed debate.
Last week's stops sit ≈20–31 bp above the 3.89% SOFR fixing, so bills already price some chance of a hike. Watch whether that premium widens or narrows.

calendar.event: Wintrust (WTFC) Q3; also W.R. Berkley, BOK Financial, F.N.B., Steel Dynamics
calendar.why: This is Chicago's biggest local bank and a premium-finance/commercial lender. Its deposit costs and loan growth test whether the KBW's six-week slide is overdone. The call is Tue at 10 AM CT.

calendar.event: $13B 20Y bond reopening (CME, Northern Trust, Abbott report before the open)
calendar.why: This is the week's first long-end supply test after a −15 bp rally. A tail would confirm the 5% 10Y still needs a concession.
Warsh gave no guidance in Bangkok. Thursday's claims (200K est.) and Friday's flash PMIs (composite 57.6 est. vs 58.4) are the last big inputs.

rates.title: 10Y drifts to ≈5.07% as oil, not inflation, leads
rates.body: The 10Y is ≈5.07% (−2 bp) and the 2Y ≈4.73%, extending last week's −15 bp rally as Brent slips ≈1.7%. The long end still carries a 1.33 pp term premium (SF Fed, Oct 15), up from 1.07 a year ago and 1.28 at the September FOMC.
rates.simple: Term premium is the extra yield investors demand for locking money up for 10 years instead of rolling short loans. It has risen because of inflation risk, war-driven energy prices and heavy government borrowing. Even if the Fed stops hiking, long-term rates on mortgages and corporate debt can stay high for that reason.

rates.title: Real yields ease off the 2.95% peak before Thursday's 5Y TIPS
rates.body: As of Oct 14 the 10Y TIPS real yield was 2.84%, down from a 2.95% high on Oct 5, the 5Y was 2.64% and the 10Y breakeven 2.35%. Thursday's $26B 5Y TIPS sale tests demand for inflation protection while Brent sits near $108.
rates.simple: A real yield is what a bond pays after inflation. TIPS are Treasuries that adjust for inflation, and the breakeven is the inflation rate the market expects. Falling real yields help gold, and with CPI at 3.7%, a 2.35% breakeven suggests investors think the current inflation is temporary.

rates.title: French riots widen the OAT–Bund spread
rates.body: The French 10Y is up ≈7 bp Monday after weekend riots with more than 2,000 arrests, and the CAC is down ≈1%. The OAT sits ≈4.86% vs the Bund at ≈3.41% (≈137 bp spread). The Gilt is ≈5.38% and the JGB 10Y ≈2.9–3.1% (sources disagree).
rates.simple: A spread is the gap between two countries' borrowing costs. A wider gap means investors see France as riskier, here because of social unrest on top of debt near 119% of GDP. Stress in Europe can push money into US Treasuries, which tends to pull US yields down.

derivatives.title: CME heads into Wednesday's earnings off record Q3 volume
derivatives.body: Q3 average daily volume was a record 29.4M contracts (+16% y/y), including 15.1M in interest-rate products (+13%) and 2.7M in energy (+16%). September alone set a record at 31.8M. Consensus is $2.98 EPS on ≈$1.71B revenue, with results Wed before the open (call 7:30 AM CT).
derivatives.simple: CME runs the exchanges where traders buy and sell futures, contracts to trade something later at a price fixed today. It earns a fee on each trade, so volatile months like this one, with Fed, war and oil swings, are good for business. Volume is the number to watch, along with whether new products keep the growth going.

derivatives.title: Vol and front-end pricing: an October hike is mostly priced out
derivatives.body: FedWatch shows ≈84% hold / ≈16% hike for Oct 28, down from ≈44% hike odds right after CPI on Oct 14. SOFR fixed 3.89% (Oct 15) vs IORB at 3.90%, and the 10Y SOFR swap was 4.71%. That puts the 10Y swap spread around −35 to −37 bp (our arithmetic). The VIX closed Friday at 19.99 and the MOVE at ≈102.5 (single source).
derivatives.simple: Fed-funds and SOFR futures let traders bet on where the Fed's rate will be, and FedWatch turns those prices into odds. A swap spread is the gap between the swap rate and the Treasury yield. A deeply negative spread means Treasuries yield more than swaps, a sign that dealers are struggling to absorb all the government debt.

derivatives.title: Brent options record, and the weekend gap that didn't come
derivatives.body: ICE Brent options set Q3 records for volume and ADV as Hormuz risk drove hedging. Monday's open went the other way: Brent fell from $109.86 to ≈$107.60–108.52 on the Russia waiver, not up on the IRGC mine claim.
derivatives.simple: An option is the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set price. Traders use options to protect against sudden jumps like a weekend tanker attack. This weekend the bigger news was more Russian supply being allowed, so anyone who paid up for upside protection lost money.

derivatives.title: CME widens its crypto lineup while fighting the CFTC on perps
derivatives.body: CME lists Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap futures today, bringing it to 11 single-asset crypto contracts, and plans European dairy futures and options. It is also suing the CFTC over the agency's approval of bitcoin perpetual futures at a rival.
derivatives.simple: A perpetual future is a futures contract that never expires, hugely popular on offshore crypto exchanges. CME argues the CFTC's approval for a competitor was improper because these products could pull trading away from CME's traditional dated futures. That is a fight over who wins the next wave of trading volume.

metals.title: Gold +0.3% to $4,175.60 as yields ease; futures test $4,200
metals.body: Spot gold is $4,175.60 and Dec futures $4,196.40 after briefly going above $4,200, following a −0.7% week. WGC data show a record $31B of Q3 ETF inflows (holdings a record 4,256t), and the PBoC added 23t in September, its largest month since Oct 2023. Gold is still ≈26% below its 2026 peak.
metals.simple: Gold pays no interest, so it does better when real interest rates fall and the dollar is flat or weaker, as this morning. Central banks, led by China, keep buying it to hold fewer dollars. That puts a floor under the price even when traders turn cautious.

metals.title: Silver and PGMs bounce 1–1.5% after a rough month
metals.body: Silver is ≈$57.5 (+≈1%; APMEX later showed $58.31) after falling ≈11% over the past month. Platinum is ≈$1,651–1,656 (+≈1.3%) and palladium ≈$1,133 (+≈1.5%).
metals.simple: Silver and platinum-group metals (PGMs: platinum and palladium) are partly precious and partly industrial, used in solar panels and car catalytic converters. They swing harder than gold. China's stronger-than-expected factory output gave them a lift today.

metals.title: LME Week opens with record-negative copper treatment charges
metals.body: LME copper is ≈$14,480/t (Fri), ≈3% below September's $14,875 record. Antofagasta cleared Centinela concentrate at −$310/t and Los Pelambres in the −$330s, with Teck's Highland Valley in the −$370s. 2027 benchmark talks with Chinese smelters start this week. Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula and El Teniente remain disrupted, and a possible 15% US refined-copper tariff from Jan 2027 is still unconfirmed.
metals.simple: Treatment charges are the fee miners normally pay smelters to turn ore into metal. When they go negative, smelters are paying miners for ore, which shows how scarce mined copper is. Tight supply plus China's 4.5% growth keeps copper near records, raising costs for wiring, power grids and data centers.

banking.title: Fifth Third beats as the Comerica integration finishes
banking.body: Q3 adjusted EPS was $1.13 ($0.90 reported) vs ≈$1.08–1.09 consensus. Net income to common was $828M vs $608M a year ago, NII $2.28B (+3% q/q), revenue ≈$3.28B and CET1 10.02%.
banking.simple: NII (net interest income) is what a bank earns on loans minus what it pays depositors, its core profit engine. CET1 is the bank's cushion of top-quality capital against losses. Fifth Third bought Comerica, and this quarter shows the merger adding earnings, a template for other regional-bank deals.

banking.title: KBW Bank Index: six straight losing weeks, longest since 2008
banking.body: Big-bank shares fell ≈1% last week, leaving the index ≈13% below its August record. BofA dropped 5.7% on a revenue miss and a $1.2B settlement charge. Regions earned $0.71 with record capital-markets fees, and PNC net income was $2.097B.
banking.simple: The KBW index tracks large US bank stocks. Investors are selling on fears that AI-related loans could sour and that hot inflation forces more Fed hikes, which can hurt loan demand. Good earnings haven't been enough to stop the slide so far.

banking.title: Regional earnings wave: Wintrust tonight, KeyCorp and Capital One Tuesday
banking.body: Wintrust is expected at $3.31 EPS / $754.7M revenue (Q2: $3.30, record $233.7M NI). KeyCorp is expected at $0.46 on ≈$2.05B. Capital One's focus is Discover card migration costs. BOK Financial, F.N.B. and ServisFirst also report this week.
banking.simple: Regional banks lend to mid-sized companies and local real estate, so their results show how Main Street is handling 5% Treasury yields. Watch deposit costs, meaning what banks pay savers, and loan growth. For Capital One, the question is whether absorbing Discover's card network is costing more than planned.

banking.title: Private credit: record fundraising, a deployment squeeze and a Barclays swap probe
banking.body: Nuveen Private Capital reached $100B, and Reuters reports private-credit fundraising at records while finding deals to fund gets harder. CNBC reported the Bank of England is examining whether Barclays traders misstated total return swaps on private-credit loans. The shares fell ≈2.5%; one source only.
banking.simple: Private credit is lending by investment funds instead of banks. A total return swap lets a bank pass the gains and losses on a loan to someone else without selling it. If those swaps were valued wrongly, losses tied to risky loans could be hiding on a bank's books, which is why regulators care.

banking.title: Quiet IPO week before a possible Anthropic filing; M&A led by tech
banking.body: Renaissance Capital lists no US IPOs this week, with an Anthropic filing possibly as soon as Friday. Last week's deals: Proofpoint–Varonis (≈$6.3B) and Copart–ACV (≈$1.9B). Byline–Illinois State Bancorp ($87.9M, Oct 6) is the latest Illinois bank deal.
banking.simple: An IPO is when a private company first sells shares to the public, and investment banks earn big fees running it. A mega-IPO like Anthropic's would be a major test of investor appetite. Small bank mergers like Byline's show community banks combining to spread rising compliance and technology costs.

cnbc.title: Futures rise as AI buyers return after the worst week since June
cnbc.body: Nasdaq futures are up ≈1% and Brent is down 1.7% to ≈$108.02 on the Russia waiver. Fed funds futures show ≈84% odds of an Oct 28 hold.
cnbc.simple: Stock futures trade overnight and preview the day's opening. After a big selloff in tech stocks, bargain hunters are stepping back in. Cheaper oil also eases inflation fears that would push the Fed to hike.

cnbc.title: French riots hit Paris stocks and bonds
cnbc.body: The CAC fell ≈1–1.2% and the French 10Y rose ≈7 bp after weekend riots with more than 2,000 arrests. The euro slipped to ≈$1.1225.
cnbc.simple: When a country looks politically unstable, investors demand more interest to lend to it and sell its stocks. France already has heavy government debt, so unrest makes markets worry about its ability to manage it.

cnbc.title: China's Q3 growth quickens to 4.5% on exports
cnbc.body: GDP grew 4.5% y/y (4.4% expected) and 1.2% q/q. Industrial output rose 5.5%, retail sales 1.1%, and FAI fell 7.2% YTD.
cnbc.simple: GDP measures an economy's total output. China grew a bit faster than expected, but mostly by selling goods abroad rather than its own people spending. That is good for metals demand, but it reduces the pressure on Beijing to stimulate.

cnbc.title: Indonesian stocks hit a six-year low on MSCI downgrade fears
cnbc.body: Indonesia's benchmark fell more than 5% Monday on fears that MSCI will cut the market's index status.
cnbc.simple: MSCI builds the indexes that trillions of dollars of funds copy. A downgrade forces those funds to sell automatically, so investors are getting out early.

wsj.title: Putin floats a Trump–Xi summit on Ukraine
wsj.body: The WSJ reports Putin proposed a three-way meeting next month without Zelensky. The Kremlin says the idea is under discussion but not settled.
wsj.simple: A peace deal would likely bring more Russian oil and gas to market, which would push energy prices down. Leaving Ukraine out of the talks makes any deal politically fragile.

wsj.title: Russian fuel waivers become a midterm liability for the GOP
wsj.body: Trump's Russian diesel license and sanctions waivers are dogging Republican candidates ahead of Nov 3, while diesel stays near record highs.
wsj.simple: Waivers let Americans buy Russian fuel despite sanctions, aimed at lowering diesel prices. Voters and allies see it as going easy on Russia, and diesel is still expensive, so it isn't helping much politically.

wsj.title: Michael Dell: the memory chip crunch will worsen
wsj.body: Dell expects the memory shortage to deepen into 2027 and called it possibly 'a four-year problem.'
wsj.simple: AI data centers are gobbling up memory chips, leaving fewer for PCs and phones. Prices for those devices may rise, and chipmakers like Micron profit.

wsj.title: Oil falls ≈2% as the Russia waiver outweighs Hormuz
wsj.body: Brent fell to ≈$107.60–108 and WTI to ≈$97.50–100. Analysts note the waiver doesn't fix the Hormuz disruption.
wsj.simple: More legal Russian supply calms fears of a shortage. But the Strait of Hormuz, where much of the world's oil passes, is still disrupted, so prices remain far above normal.

tribune.title: Wintrust reports after the close
tribune.body: Consensus is $3.31 EPS (vs $3.06 a year ago) on ≈$754.7M revenue, after a record Q2 profit of $233.7M.
tribune.simple: Wintrust is Chicago's largest locally based bank. Its results show how local businesses and borrowers are coping with high interest rates.

tribune.title: CME adds Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap futures
tribune.body: The launch brings CME to 11 single-asset crypto contracts. CME also plans European dairy futures and reports Q3 Wednesday after record September ADV of 31.8M.
tribune.simple: The Chicago exchange keeps adding products so more traders bring their business to it. Crypto futures let big institutions bet on digital coins through a regulated exchange.

tribune.title: United Airlines reports Tuesday with fuel the swing factor
tribune.body: Analysts expect ≈$3.03 EPS within the $2.50–3.50 guide. Fuel added ≈$575M of cost in Q3.
tribune.simple: Jet fuel is an airline's second-biggest cost after labor. With oil around $100, investors want to know how much United can pass on through higher fares.

tribune.title: Goolsbee: AI build-out may be overheating the economy
tribune.body: The Chicago Fed president called September CPI 'discouraging' but wants more data before backing another hike. The policy range is 3.75–4.00%.
tribune.simple: Massive spending on AI data centers is pushing up demand for power, construction and chips, which can raise prices. Goolsbee is signaling patience, not an automatic hike.

tribune.title: Diesel costs squeeze Chicago's less visible businesses
tribune.body: US diesel averaged ≈$6.28/gal around Oct 8, up ≈70% since the war began Feb 28. That pressures truckers, distributors and contractors in the Chicago area.
tribune.simple: Diesel powers trucks, trains and construction equipment, so its price feeds into almost everything that gets shipped. Small firms can't hedge it the way airlines can.

nyt.title: US floats reviving Russian gas transit through Ukraine
nyt.body: The NYT reports US officials proposed, as part of a peace framework, that the EU buy more Russian gas and that Ukraine allow transit again.
nyt.simple: Europe cut Russian gas after the invasion and pays more for alternatives. Reopening the pipeline would cut European energy costs but hand Russia revenue and leverage.

nyt.title: France's worst riots in years expose fiscal risk
nyt.body: The OAT 10Y is at ≈4.86% vs the Bund at 3.41%, with French debt near 119% of GDP.
nyt.simple: France borrows a lot, and unrest makes painful budget fixes harder. That is why its borrowing cost is well above Germany's.

nyt.title: Warsh keeps markets guessing before Oct 28
nyt.body: October hike odds fell below ≈15–20% from ≈27% after his Bangkok remarks. Goldman expects a skip now and a hike in December, with CPI at 3.7%.
nyt.simple: By refusing to give guidance, the Fed chair keeps traders uncertain. Markets now think the Fed waits this month but may still raise rates by year-end.

talking_points.point: With the 10Y SOFR swap ≈4.71% vs the 10Y Treasury ≈5.07–5.09%, the 10Y swap spread is about −35 to −37 bp (my arithmetic off public quotes). Ask a rates desk whether that reflects dealer balance-sheet limits (SLR) as coupon supply grows, and whether the SLR changes have made swap-spread wideners a real trade into the November refunding.

talking_points.topic: Copper: negative TCs vs. a futures discount to the record
talking_points.point: Antofagasta's spot charges at −$310 to −$370/t mean smelters are paying miners for concentrate, yet LME copper is ≈3% below its $14,875 record. A good metals question for LME Week: is the physical tightness showing up in the LME spreads/backwardation and the COMEX–LME arb (tariff risk from Jan 2027) rather than in the outright price?

talking_points.topic: CME's print as a vol barometer
talking_points.point: CME's record Q3 ADV of 29.4M (rates 15.1M) came during a Fed hiking cycle, a war and $110 Brent. Before Wednesday, ask whether consensus of $2.98 already captures the rate-per-contract mix, and how much the perp-futures fight with the CFTC and its 11-coin crypto lineup matter next to Treasury and SOFR futures, which still drive the franchise.

caveats: WSJ, NYT and the Chicago Tribune couldn't be accessed, and direct page fetches failed (DNS errors), so all figures come from search-result excerpts; WSJ and NYT items are cited via other outlets as marked. Futures, yields, metals and oil are early-session reads from different times and outlets, shown as ≈ or ranges. The Russell and Dow futures levels weren't found. The IRGC tanker-mine claim remains unconfirmed. The MOVE (≈102.5) and the Barclays TRS probe each rest on a single source. The swap spread is our own calculation. Fifth Third's consensus varies by aggregator. Canada CPI consensus wasn't found.

updates.label: Close
updates.headline: Tech's rebound held but halved into the bell (Nasdaq +1.11%, S&P +0.41%, Dow −0.07%), and the long end kept cheapening: the 30Y finished ≈5.45% against a ≈5.08% 10Y. Wintrust and Zions report tonight.
points: Final levels (CNBC): S&P 500 7,690.73 (+0.41%), Nasdaq Comp 26,430.89 (+1.11%), Dow 51,966.03 (−36.38, −0.07%). At midday the S&P was ≈+0.8% and the Nasdaq ≈+1.6%, so roughly half the gain faded. Chips led all day (Bloomberg had a chip gauge +3.5% at midday). This was dip-buying after the Nasdaq's −4.5% week, not a broad re-rating. Meta and Tesla later this week are the real test of the AI trade.

Rates (approximate; no official close in reach): 10Y ≈5.08% (≈−1 bp), 2Y ≈4.76%, 30Y ≈5.44–5.47% (≈+2–4 bp) per Trading Economics. That's 2s30s ≈70 bp: a mild bear-steepener into Wednesday's $13B 20Y. The morning's '10Y slipped to ≈5.07%' read held but didn't extend. The market still prices an Oct 28 hold, and LSEG had a December hike at ≈88% (Friday read; not refreshed today). Axios flagged unusual Treasury volatility: last week's hot CPI briefly pushed the 10Y over 5.3%.

Commodities: oil stayed lower on the Russia waiver, with Brent ≈$107.6–108.4 (≈−1.5–2% vs the $109.86 Fri settle) and WTI ≈$97.5–99.5. I couldn't confirm settles. Gold Dec futures were $4,163.40 (−$17.70, −0.42%) at 2:33 PM CT (Yahoo), with spot ≈$4,168–4,181. Silver outperformed again at ≈$58.2 spot (+0.8%, USAGOLD), and COMEX copper was $6.54/lb (+0.16%, Trading Economics).

Banks: I found no new bank M&A today. After the close: Wintrust (est. $3.31 EPS / $754.7M revenue; Q2 was $3.30 with a 3.52% NIM), Zions, W.R. Berkley, BOK Financial, F.N.B. and Steel Dynamics. The 26-wk bill drew a 2.84 bid-to-cover vs a 2.74 average, so demand was ordinary. I couldn't find the 13-wk result.

Tuesday (CT): Sep housing starts at 7:30 AM (1.30M est vs 1.275M prior) and the KC Fed manufacturing survey at 10 AM. Pre-market earnings: GE, GM, RTX, 3M, Northrop, Halliburton, Ally, MSCI. After the close: Netflix, Capital One, Intuitive Surgical, Chubb, United. The Wintrust call is at 10 AM. The Fed is still in blackout.
updates.simple: Tech stocks finished higher but gave back about half their morning gains, a sign that investors are cautiously buying the dip rather than fully confident. Long-term government bonds kept falling in price, so their yields (the interest they pay) rose. Thirty-year borrowing costs are now well above ten-year ones, and that gap (a 'steeper curve') usually means investors want extra pay to lend for decades. That keeps mortgage and long-term business loan rates high, but it helps banks, which earn the gap between short-term deposits and longer-term loans. Tonight's results from Chicago's Wintrust will show whether that benefit is reaching the bank's profits.

updates.label: Midday
updates.headline: The tech rebound broadened into midday (S&P ≈+0.8%, Nasdaq ≈+1.5–1.7%), but the long end is cheapening: the 30Y is up ≈1.5 bp to ≈5.45% while the 2Y sits flat at ≈4.73%, so the curve is bear-steepening into Wednesday's 20Y.
points: Stocks at ≈11 AM CT: S&P 500 ≈7,721–7,725 (+0.8%), Nasdaq Comp ≈26,576 (+1.5–1.7%), Dow ≈52,094 (+0.15%), VIX ≈18 (Motley Fool, 24/7 Wall St., Sunday Guardian). Correction to the Post-open note: the Russell 2000's −1.66% was Friday's move, not today's. A mid-morning read had it ≈2,726, +0.2% (Investrade), so small caps are flat rather than collapsing. The 'megacap-only' point still holds.

Rates: the 10Y is ≈5.08% (−1 bp) and the 2Y ≈4.73% (flat) per Trading Economics, but the 30Y is ≈5.45% (+1.5 bp, Investrade) vs the ≈5.41% morning read. That puts 2s30s near 72 bp. The morning's 'term premium' thesis is intact: supply-sensitive long-end paper isn't joining the rally. Today's 26-wk bill drew a 2.84 bid-to-cover (in line); the stop rates weren't published in sources I could reach.

Oil: WTI ≈$98.4 (≈−3% vs the $101.41 settle) and Brent ≈$108.6 (≈−1.2%) per Yahoo/ZeroHedge snapshots. The Russia waiver is still the driver. The unconfirmed IRGC tanker-mine claims haven't produced a squeeze, and Hormuz traffic trackers still show the strait effectively shut.

Metals and the dollar: spot gold has slipped to ≈$4,146 (−0.5%) per Invezz, below the ≈$4,163 Post-open read. Lower oil cools breakevens, the DXY is firmer at ≈101.93 (+0.1%), and that combination is hitting gold. Silver is ≈$57.1–57.2 (+0.2–0.3%), off the $58 morning print. COMEX copper is ≈$6.57–6.59/lb.
No new bank M&A today. Wintrust (≈$3.31 EPS est.) still reports after the close. FedWatch odds weren't refreshed (morning: ≈84% hold for Oct 28).
updates.simple: Big tech stocks keep recovering from last week's sell-off. But long-term government bonds are falling in price, which pushes their yields (the interest they pay) higher, even as short-term yields hold steady. When long-term borrowing costs rise faster than short-term ones (a 'steepening' curve), investors are usually asking for extra pay to hold debt for decades. That matters for mortgages and for banks, which borrow short and lend long. Gold slipped because cheaper oil eases inflation fears and a slightly stronger dollar makes gold pricier for foreign buyers.

updates.label: Post-open
updates.headline: Megacap tech is leading the rebound (Nasdaq ≈+1.1%, S&P ≈+0.6%), but small caps are getting crushed (Russell ≈−1.7%) as NAHB sinks to 29, a 14-year low, and the 10Y holds just under 5.08%.
points: Cash open (TheStreet, ≈8:58 AM CT): S&P 500 +0.57%, Nasdaq Comp +1.09%, Dow −0.08%, Russell 2000 −1.66%. The morning call of Russell futures ≈+0.5% was wrong. Today is a megacap-only bounce, not a broad risk-on day, and that's a poor setup for regional banks ahead of Wintrust tonight.

NAHB Oct HMI 29 vs 31 consensus and 32 prior (Trading Economics; not yet confirmed by NAHB). It's the second straight drop and the lowest since June 2012. With the 10Y near 5.08%, housing is the clearest growth-scare signal in the data.

Rates: the 10Y is at 5.079%, ≈−1 bp (CNBC), close to one-month lows. That's slightly higher than the ≈5.07% morning read, so the pre-market rally hasn't extended. Canada Sep CPI came in at 3.1% y/y vs 3.2% expected (2.2% ex-gasoline, CPI-trim 1.8%), a soft G10 print. Still to come: $95B 13-wk and $82B 26-wk bills at 10:30 AM CT.

Oil keeps sliding on the Russia waiver: Brent $107.57 (Reuters, 0619 GMT) and WTI below $97 (FXStreet, European morning) vs Fri settles of $109.86 and $101.41. Rubio said there's a 60-day review. Counterpoint: reports now say three tankers were damaged near Hormuz over the weekend, and VLCC freight is at a record.

Metals: gold has given back its overnight gain and is ≈flat at $4,163 spot (JM Bullion, 8:49 AM CT; CNBC $4,161.54 at 8 AM CT), back below the $4,200 Dec-futures print. Silver is holding up better at $58.03, +$0.63.
updates.simple: Big tech stocks are bouncing after last week's sell-off, but smaller companies, which borrow more and are more sensitive to interest rates, are falling hard. A survey of home builders dropped to its lowest level since 2012 because mortgage rates tied to the ≈5% 10-year Treasury yield (the interest the government pays to borrow for 10 years) are keeping buyers away. Oil keeps easing after the US paused new sanctions on Russian oil, which takes some pressure off inflation, and in turn off the Fed.
